clue.text: Aussie town in which firm's controlled by Conservative politician's helper

indicators.note: the town's name is opened up so the other pieces sit inside it

parts.note: Alice Springs, the Australian outback town, is called Alice for short

indicators.note: the firm sits beneath and after its controlling Conservative in the run of letters

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A politician's aide caught up in a corrupt Australian company deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in which' signals the container; 'controlled by' keeps the firm after the Conservative. Alice Springs is the town in Australia's Northern Territory.
explanation.definitionFit: An accomplice is a partner who assists in a crime, a kind of helper.

clue.text: Uncommonly bad opening for article, agreed? It's discarded

indicators.note: the scrambled letters open up to make room for the article and the agreement
uncommonly suggests the letters of bad appear in an unusual order

parts.note: AN is the indefinite article
'Done!' is said to seal a deal, meaning agreed

explanation.surface: An odd query about whether a bad start was agreed, then it was scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncommonly' gives ABD, which 'opening for' splits after its second letter. 'Done!' is how a bargain is agreed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abandoned has been given up or thrown aside, i.e. discarded.

clue.text: The men sounded cocky

definitions.meaning: the group of men working a ship or job
a past tense of crow, the call a cock makes

explanation.definitionFit: A crew is a team of workers; a cockerel that crowed is said to have crew in older English.

clue.text: Contend small child must receive illuminated address, firstly

indicators.note: the child's word takes the other pieces into its middle

parts.note: a mite is a small child
lit means illuminated

indicators.note: firstly asks only for the opening letter of address

explanation.surface: A tiny child has to take in a lit-up speech before arguing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must receive' makes the child's word the container, and 'firstly' takes only the A of 'address'.
explanation.definitionFit: To militate is to argue or work against something, to contend.

clue.text: Student element required to assimilate a classical subject

parts.note: L is a learner driver, a student
tin is a chemical element

explanation.surface: A student must absorb some element of the classics.
explanation.walkthrough: L (the learner plate) then TIN with A inside it: L + T(A)IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin, the language of ancient Rome, is studied as one of the classics.

clue.text: Woollen garment put on by a chap, originally a heart patient

indicators.note: the garment is followed by what puts it on, joining the pieces in order

parts.note: a cardi is short for cardigan, a woollen garment

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of chap

explanation.surface: A man pulls on a cardigan, originally a cardiac patient.
explanation.walkthrough: CARDI + A + C (first letter of 'chap').
explanation.definitionFit: A cardiac, used as a noun, is a person with heart disease.

clue.text: Utensils supplied for meal are new, specially ordered

indicators.note: these letters are put into a special new order

explanation.surface: New kitchen things have been specially ordered for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'specially ordered' rearranges MEAL ARE NEW.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamelware is enamelled metal kitchenware: pots, pans and other utensils.

clue.text: Views given by German people

definitions.meaning: the ... were a Germanic tribe who settled in England

explanation.definitionFit: Angles are viewpoints; the Angles were a Germanic people who gave England its name.

clue.text: Apple variety from Nepal? No, Rhode Island, surprisingly

indicators.note: surprisingly hints at an unexpected arrangement of these letters

parts.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: An apple that turns out to come from Rhode Island, not Nepal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges NEPAL + NO + RI.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonpareil is the name of an old variety of apple.

clue.text: In fact I regularly suffer reduction in interest

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone admits they routinely lose interest.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'facT I REgularly'. 'regularly' looks like an alternate-letters signal, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To tire of something is to grow bored with it, losing interest.

clue.text: Girl catching boy's infection, possibly

indicators.note: the girl's name catches, or holds, the boy inside it

parts.note: May is a girl's name
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A girl picks up her boyfriend's bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' reads as catching an illness, but here the girl's name holds the boy.
explanation.definitionFit: An illness or disease is a malady, and an infection is one example.

clue.text: Erect bearing

definitions.meaning: status or reputation, the position one holds in society

explanation.definitionFit: Standing means upright, and also one's status or position in the eyes of others.

clue.text: Rich, parsimonious, happy medium?

parts.note: golden can mean rich or lavish, as in golden opportunity
mean means stingy

explanation.surface: A question of whether someone can be wealthy and stingy yet content.
explanation.walkthrough: The golden mean is Aristotle's idea of virtue as the moderate path between extremes.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden mean is the desirable middle course between two extremes.

clue.text: Having no success finding error in record book

indicators.note: the wrongdoing sits inside the record book

parts.note: a log is a book of records, like a ship's log
a sin is an error or wrongdoing

explanation.surface: A failure is traced to a mistake in the ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; 'finding' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing means failing to win, having no success.

clue.text: A clay-pit worked out? That's unusual

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a fresh arrangement, like an exhausted pit

explanation.surface: A clay pit that is worked out is rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked out' rearranges A CLAY-PIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Atypical means not representative of the type, so unusual.

clue.text: Cat's-paw seen to behave timidly?

parts.note: a pussy is a cat
a paw is an animal's foot

explanation.surface: A dupe, or cat's-paw, is seen as timid.
explanation.walkthrough: A cat's-paw is a person used as a tool by another, which makes the whole phrase look like a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pussyfoot is to act cautiously and avoid commitment, being timid.

clue.text: Scramble in which man's caught in pincer movement

indicators.note: the man is trapped inside the rearranged letters
movement signals that the letters of pincer move about

parts.note: he refers to a man

explanation.surface: A man gets trapped in a military pincer movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movement' rearranges the pincer letters to ENCIPR, and 'caught in' places the man between the P and the R.
explanation.definitionFit: To encipher a message is to put it into code, scrambling it.

clue.text: Worker accepting two hairstyles should be ample?

indicators.note: the insect takes the hairstyles into its middle

parts.note: the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker
a bun is a hairstyle with hair coiled at the back
DA, short for duck's arse, is a 1950s slicked-back hairstyle

explanation.surface: A worker with two hairdos is asking whether that is plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepting' signals the container. DA (duck's arse) is the British name for the swept-back quiff of 1950s rockers.
explanation.definitionFit: Abundant means plentiful, more than enough.

clue.text: A service heartless pawnbroker's first to forget

indicators.note: first places the pawnbroker's piece at the front
the middle letter is taken out of the pawnbroker's nickname

parts.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker
RN, the Royal Navy, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A heartless pawnbroker learns to forget a service.
explanation.walkthrough: UNCLE without its middle C gives UNLE, which comes first, then A and RN.
explanation.definitionFit: To unlearn something is to deliberately forget it.

clue.text: Vehicle in excellent condition

parts.note: E is a mark for excellent in some grading schemes
state means condition

explanation.surface: A car described as in top shape.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate is the British name for a station wagon, a car with a large rear load area.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate car is a type of motor vehicle.

clue.text: Type of acid making ice act unpredictably

indicators.note: unpredictably means the letters of ice act fall out of order

explanation.surface: An acid that makes ice behave oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unpredictably' rearranges ICE ACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetic acid is the acid found in vinegar.

clue.text: City playing Celtic, exemplifying different styles?

parts.note: EC is the postcode for the City of London

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of Celtic are being moved around

explanation.surface: A city team playing Celtic shows varied tactics.
explanation.walkthrough: Celtic is a Glasgow football club. EC is the City of London postcode, and 'playing' rearranges CELTIC to LECTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclectic means drawing on a wide range of sources or tastes.

clue.text: Knitting pattern sailor left in church?

indicators.note: the sailor and the left sit inside the church abbreviation

parts.note: CE stands for Church of England
AB is an able seaman, a sailor

explanation.surface: A knitting pattern left by a sailor in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container; CE (Church of England) is the church in the Anglican sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Cable stitch is a raised twisted pattern in knitting.

clue.text: Where you'd have found Greek philosopher solving my clue?

definitions.text: Where you'd have found Greek philosopher

indicators.note: solving the clue means unravelling its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks where an ancient thinker would solve a crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solving' rearranges MY CLUE. The Lyceum was the school in Athens where Aristotle taught.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle taught in the Lyceum, a gymnasium outside ancient Athens.

clue.text: Not charged, hence at liberty

explanation.definitionFit: Free means costing nothing, and also not held captive.

clue.text: Boast about period dress

indicators.note: about tells us the boast is turned around

parts.note: brag means boast

explanation.surface: Bragging about vintage costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns BRAG around.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is clothing, especially the distinctive dress of a time or role.

clue.text: Girl's after musical instrument — not piano, wind instrument

indicators.note: after places the girl's name behind the shortened instrument
not drops the letter for piano from the instrument

parts.note: the harp is a musical instrument
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
Monica is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl takes up a different instrument, not piano.
explanation.walkthrough: HARP without P gives HAR, followed by MONICA.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica, or mouth organ, is played by blowing into it.

clue.text: Expensive pieces must be entrusted to English conservation body, sweetie-pie

indicators.note: the valuable pieces are placed inside, held in the body's care

parts.note: NT is the National Trust, which conserves historic properties
dear means costly
chessmen are pieces, so men

explanation.surface: Costly items handed to the National Trust, darling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be entrusted to' puts the costly pieces inside E plus NT. The National Trust is a British charity looking after historic houses.
explanation.definitionFit: An endearment is an affectionate term such as sweetie-pie.
